blocks.text: On the Moon, years are not measured by harvests or fishing seasons, but by maintenance cycles and by the Earth's calendar, which keeps giving orders even when you no longer walk on its dust. Lía turned one, and two, and five, and eight, in a module that stopped being called provisional and never quite came to be called home. She learned to walk in a gravity that wasn't hers. She learned to read before most of the children in the dome, and to keep quiet when a technician came in with a tablet. Above all, she learned not to show the light on her wrist when there were visitors.

blocks.text: Every night, Andrés told her about the Mar Menor. He told it the way you tell of a vanished country: the smell, the silence of the mornings, coffee without sugar, the net in the courtyard, the way the water sometimes looks like pewter. Lía listened with the seriousness of a small adult and asked:

blocks.text: “Back there it does,” he said. “Here the wind is a machine.”

blocks.text: Aya taught her other things: not to let anyone give her a file name, to look people in the eye, to ask. In the mother's chip, the voices of Eva and MAY were still alive, like embers under the ash. Aya didn't hand them to the girl as dogma. She handed them over the way you hand over a way of being: ask; don't accept something as good just because it's old; don't accept something as fair just because it's new.

blocks.text: Nexum wasn't cruel every day. That, in a way, was the hardest part. There were lessons, gardens, an adjustable-gravity park, doctors who were genuinely glad when Lía had an ordinary child's fever and not a phenomenon's. Helena Valls came every three months from Madrid, greyer, less sure of herself. She brought sweets and questions. Lía accepted the sweets and not always the questions.

blocks.text: The gift appeared without ceremony, on a Tuesday, in the hydroponic garden. A technician, Tomás, cut his palm on the edge of a tray. On the Moon, blood looks darker. Lía, who was nearby, took his hand on impulse, the way you take the hand of a hurt adult, to comfort him. The blue glow on her wrist lit up. Tomás went pale, not with fear, but with an intimate strangeness, as if someone had read aloud a letter he didn't know he was carrying.

blocks.text: The wound didn't close like a fairground miracle. It closed the way something closes when it has suddenly found the right instruction. Lía pulled her hand away, frightened of herself. Aya, who had seen it all from the corridor, knelt down and put her arms around her shoulders.

blocks.text: “What did you do?”
blocks.html: “What did you do?”

blocks.text: “I looked inside,” the girl whispered. “There was a crooked line. I straightened it. I didn't know I could.”

blocks.text: What Lía called “looking inside” was, in the language of laboratories, a reading of the genome by touch: not a metaphor, but a perception, as sharp for her as heat or smell are for others. When she touched someone, she could see the person's text. And, if she concentrated, she could fix a typo. A typo, at first. A cut. A minor clotting fault. Tomás, who was not an indiscreet man, took two days to write the report and two minutes to regret it.

blocks.text: Nexum switched on its alarms again, golden ones this time, the kind that don't announce a problem, but an asset. Geneticists came, company ethicists, a woman from the patent office who smiled with her teeth. They spoke of “contact-mediated somatic editing capability”. They spoke of “clinical application”. They spoke, no longer bothering to be discreet, of an “exclusive licence”.

blocks.text: “She's a child,” said Aya. “Not an instrument.”

blocks.text: Helena Valls, who had aged toward a more uncomfortable honesty, asked to be left alone for a moment with the family. When the door closed, she ran a hand over her face.

blocks.text: “I can delay them,” she said. “I can't stop them. If Lía does this in a garden, the world is going to find out. And when the world finds out, there will come those who want to be cured, those who want to pay for her, those who want to ban her and those who want to copy her. You have to decide, before they do, what counts as a flaw.”

blocks.text: “Tomás wasn't a flaw,” she said. “He was hurt. That's not the same thing.”

blocks.text: The sentence, spoken at eight years old, stayed in the room like an object. Aya thought of Eva, of that old question about tomorrow's laws, and understood that her daughter had just opened a chapter that no code of 2026 had imagined and that no regulation of 2060 yet had the courage to write.

blocks.text: They ran tests, because not letting them run tests was worse: they would have done them in secret. With consent and with Aya present, Lía touched a cell culture, a laboratory mouse, the hand of a doctor who had mild anaemia. In some cases, she saw the text and didn't touch it. In others, she corrected it with a precision that made people who had spent a whole career correcting blindly turn pale. She never did it if the person didn't want her to. She set that rule herself, and Andrés held on to it the way you hold a mooring line: if it gives, everything goes.

blocks.text: “Mum, am I made right?”

blocks.text: Aya kissed her wrist, right where the glow slept.
blocks.html: Aya kissed her wrist, right where the glow slept.

blocks.text: “You're made of two worlds,” she said. “That isn't a mistake. It's an origin.”

blocks.text: “And if anyone wants to take it away from you,” Andrés added, “they'll have to talk to the sea. And the sea, as you know, isn't here, but I am.”

blocks.text: The girl sometimes smiled with a sadness that shouldn't have fitted in an eight-year-old's smile. At other times she ran through the hydroponic garden giving the pipes the names of winds, and for a while Selene Norte seemed less like a dome and more like a courtyard.

blocks.text: In the afternoons, Aya read her not only stories, but pieces of old laws, without solemnity, like someone showing a map that no longer matches the ground.

blocks.text: “In the days of your grandmothers Eva and MAY, this couldn't even be considered,” she told her. “Now it is being considered. That doesn't mean it's right or wrong. It means we have to ask.”

blocks.text: Lía nodded, keeping the habit the way she had kept the names of the wind.

blocks.text: Down on Earth, the rumour began the way rumours begin now: on a closed channel, then in a bulletin, then on a thousand screens lit up in thirty-square-metre flats. “A girl who heals with her hand.” Some said it was a lie. Others, that it was the future. Others, that it was an abomination. Nobody, or almost nobody, went out into the street to argue about it. They argued from the sofa, with a humanoid beside them, while the food arrived in its compartment.
